The syllable is proposed as the tone-bearing unit, as has been similarly noted by Stirtz (2014b). new_statements.quote: As in related languages, Lopit is analyzed to have two underlying level tones, High and Low, as in hɔ̀y 'you sg.' and hɔ́y 'us'. Contour tone consists of more than one level tone on the same syllable. The syllable is the tone-bearing unit, and at most two tones are allowed on the same syllable. Rising tone such as in hɔ̌yt 'bones' and bɛ̀lyɛ̌ 'skin' is rare. Falling tone is common on the final syllable of words, but rare elsewhere, as in bɔ̂rɛ̀ 'stable' and hɔ̀fît-tî 'hair-sg.' The lexical function of tone is low in that there are few tone minimal pairs. The grammatical distinctions of case and noun plural formation can be made solely by tone, and are discussed in section 1.8.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has Lopit with an empty rule and no statements; this work establishes that the language is tonal (two level tones, syllable TBU, low lexical load, grammatical tone for case/number) and is silent on stress. The task's open_url (https://www.sil.org) was only the site root; the item is SIL archive 57435.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lopit (Ngotira dialect) is analysed as a two-level tone language (H, L; syllable is the TBU; contours = two tones on one syllable; falling tone common word-finally, rising rare); tone carries little lexical load but marks case and noun number. Nothing is said about word stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the paper (the words do not occur).
new_statements.identity_note: Stirtz 2014 analyses the Ngotira dialect of Lopit and compares it with Dorik, Lomiaha, Lohutok and Lolongo (Ngabori not represented); the Grammar Book is pan-dialectal (authors from Dorik, Ngotira, Lomiaha, Lohutok and Lolongo) and states (p. 44 fn. 5) that no Lopit dialect has a vowel length distinction. Earlier phonologies cited by Stirtz (Turner 2001, Lolongo; Moodie 2012, Dorik) and the Brill grammar Moodie & Billington 2020 were not among the listed open works.
